They’re great in an emergency, but they’re also essential tailgating and camping equipment. We chose the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 as our best overall pick, but there are plenty of options to fit your specific neeeds.

As an avid outdoorsman, I’ve had the opportunity to test a wide range of outdoor gear, including mobile and off-grid electrification equipment like solar-powered generators, as well as inverter and dual-fuel generators. These became particularly essential when the pandemic forced my travels to become domestic rather than international, which prompted me to outfit a van for long-term road-tripping.

To bring my work along for the ride, I needed a constant portable power source to charge my laptop, a portable fridge, lighting, and a myriad of devices and tools … even electric bikes. As a result, I’ve tried all the leading portable power stations (and plenty that aren’t leading, too), so I know precisely what separates the best from the blah. I’ve written all about it (and other outdoor tech) for publications, including the Daily Beast, Thrillist, the Manual, Popular Science, and more. There were cases when my own opinion resulted in a tie, so I looked to reviews from actual customers to determine which solar generators delivered the most satisfaction to the most users. The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2, Explorer 1000 v2 and Explorer 300 v2 joined the list in November 2026 based on their published specs and how they stack up against the units we’ve tested; we haven’t put any of them through our own testing yet.

If you’re thinking about dropping big money on a solar generator, consider shopping on big shopping holidays like Amazon Prime Day or Black Friday. These are expensive devices, and they experience their largest discounts around those times. That said, they frequently sell below list price, even when it’s not a retail holiday, so click through to find out.

The solar generators on this list span a wide range of budgets, from a few hundred dollars to a few thousand. They cover several uses, from camping to backup for your home. Only you know all the factors that make one of these the best solar generator for you, but we think that one of these will get the job done.

Why it made the cut: No other solar generator delivers such an excellent balance of portability, capacity, and performance.

There are a lot of excellent solar generators on this list, many of which are competitive rivals for the top spot, but none offer such an excellent fusion of capacity, portability, and well-considered design as the Bluetti Elite 200 V2. With a capacity of 2,073 watt-hours, it hits the sweet spot that will deliver on the needs of the vast majority of users.

At the same time, its compact dimensions make it easy to fit almost anywhere, though at 53.4 pounds it’s a two-hand lift. That makes it an easy pick for packing in a trunk while heading outdoors, storing in a closet for backup power, or simply having around for a convenient, mobile power source.

It also offers high output for its size. Its 2,600W running output was already hefty enough, and Bluetti’s Power Lifting mode can run resistive loads such as kettles and hair dryers at up to 3,900W. Its 1000W solar input capacity equips it for a large solar panel array, and its 1,800W wall input capacity will charge it from zero to full in about 1.4 hours, according to Bluetti.

While power station apps are notoriously glitchy, the Bluetti app is user-friendly and allows for remote monitoring and adjustment. Most users will find it has plenty of ports, including four AC ports, USB-A and USB-C ports, and a 120W car port, though there is no 30A or 50A RV plug.

I’ve found that its squared-off design is ideal for fitting into a tight storage space or building into a small van conversion. The LiFePO4 battery has a lifespan of over 6,000 cycles, and the whole unit feels plenty durable. Indeed, I have knocked my test unit around more than a little. It seems no worse for wear.

For most mid-sized portable power purposes, the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 does pretty much everything right.

Why it made the cut: The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 keeps the 2kWh capacity that made the old Explorer 2000 Plus our former top pick and drops about 20 pounds doing it.

At 39.5 pounds, the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 is a 2,042Wh LiFePO4 station one person can lift into a hatchback without planning the move. Jackery rates it for 2,200W of continuous output and 4,400W surge, enough for a full-size fridge, a microwave or most corded tools. It refills from a wall outlet in about 1.7 hours, and Jackery says it keeps about 95 percent of its charge after 12 months in storage, so it can sit in a closet between outages.

The weight savings cost you the 2000 Plus’s expansion option. Jackery says the v2 doesn’t take expansion batteries, so 2,042Wh is what you get. If you need room to grow, the EcoFlow Delta 3 Ultra Plus below is the better fit.

Why it made the cut: The EcoFlow Delta 3 Ultra Plus itself is high-capacity, high-output, and exceptionally well-designed, and can expand up to 11kWh.

The EcoFlow Delta 3 Ultra Plus is a solid contender for “best overall,” and the only reason it didn’t get it is because it’s more of a power station than most people need. But if you do need more power station, it delivers.

The standalone unit’s 3,072Wh capacity is plenty for powering an RV or van conversion, an off-grid worksite, or a home during a blackout. Its 3,600W output can run most household devices and larger appliances, EcoFlow’s X-Boost mode lets it run some higher-wattage resistive appliances at reduced voltage, and its 7,200W surge capacity handles the spike when an air conditioner, appliance, or power tool switches on. It has six charging options, and a wall outlet alone gets it to 80 percent in about 89 minutes if you’re readying for a storm or trip. Storm Guard Mode will monitor the weather and charge the unit automatically if severe weather is coming.

All that’s great, but what I really like about it is how much consideration went into various design elements. For example, whoever thought of having the rear port doors slide into protective slots is a genius. It’s a heavy unit, but the sturdy handle and telescoping wheels make it easy to move around. It’s equipped with a 30A outlet so it can plug directly into an RV, and a good number of other ports.

Excellent all around. If you need a larger, potentially expandable solar generator that offers a good dose of portability, it’s hard to beat.

Why it made the cut: The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 covers a weekend of car-camping loads at about 24 pounds, small enough to ride on the floor behind the front seat.

Car camping runs on small, steady loads: a 12V cooler, phone and headlamp charging, maybe a string of lights. The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 has 1,070Wh of LiFePO4 battery for that, and Jackery rates the cells for 4,000 cycles before they drop to 70 percent capacity. Its 1,500W inverter (3,000W surge) also handles an electric kettle at the campsite.

Two of Jackery’s 200W SolarSaga panels plug straight into its two DC ports, which is the full 400 watts it accepts. Jackery quotes about 7.5 hours to refill it from a single 200W panel, so plan on most of a sunny day if you bring just one.

Why it made the cut: Huge expandability, excellent performance, and unsurpassed solar capability make the Bluetti Apex 300 a must for reliable off-grid power.

Bluetti’s Apex 300 does everything you can find in the best off-grid solar generators, then takes it a step further. It has huge storage capacity that gets bigger and bigger depending on your needs (and budget, since all those batteries certainly aren’t cheap). You can scale up its output wattage to handle pretty much anything you throw at it. While it’s definitely very heavy, once you’ve got it in place, it’s also very intuitive to operate. Amazon sells it bundled with Bluetti’s B300K expansion battery, which doubles the standalone 2,764.8Wh capacity to 5,529.6Wh.

But where the Apex 300 truly excels is in its solar input capacity. Its standard dual 1,200W solar input is already great in its own right, but when you add on the SolarX 4K, it adds up to 4,000W more. Bluetti says a system of three Apex 300 units, each with a SolarX 4K, takes up to 19,200W of solar, enough for a serious off-grid array.

Why it made the cut: Great specs and portability, plus Jackery’s ZeroDrain reliability, make the HomePower 3000 a safe bet for outages.

From my experience, the most important thing you need from a solar generator for home backup is reliability. I’ve been disappointed more than once to find that my power station hasn’t held its charge while in storage. To that end, the Jackery HomePower 3000, equipped with its ZeroDrain tech, which Jackery says helps it hold a charge in storage, is ready when you need it. The HomePower series is a new divergence from Jackery’s already popular Explorer series, and it moves the brand forward in terms of offering not only the aforementioned ZeroDrain, but more capacity and performance for its size.

Slightly smaller and lighter than Jackery’s older Explorer 2000 Plus, it nevertheless has 1,000Wh more capacity, and it’s significantly smaller than the 3000 Pro while delivering comparable capacity and performance. That, combined with its ZeroDrain shelf life, makes it ideal for keeping in a dry closet or garage until the next outage.

Why it made the cut: Its sodium-ion battery lets the Bluetti Pioneer Na charge at 5°F, well below the point where most lithium-based power stations stop accepting a charge.

Bluetti has been making some of the best lithium-based power stations out there, and now it sells what it bills as the first commercially available sodium-ion portable power station. Typically, power stations operate poorly in cold temperatures, and store in the cold even worse. The Pioneer Na, however, can charge at temperatures as low as 5°F and discharge as low as -13°F, according to Bluetti. Most lithium-based stations can still discharge below freezing, but they usually can’t charge there, which is the bigger problem on a cold trip.

At the same time, the performance is good. While the 900Wh capacity isn’t massive, it’s plenty for smaller-scale uses like camping or short-term backup power during an outage. And the 1,500W output is more than enough to power a fridge, TV, and a handful of devices at once. I’m also a big fan of its zippy charging, as Bluetti says it reaches 80 percent in 35 minutes, and full in 52, with 1,900 watts of combined wall and solar input. For weathering the cold, it’s the one to get.

Why it made the cut: The Jackery Explorer 300 v2 keeps the original’s small footprint but moves to a LiFePO4 battery that Jackery rates for 4,000 cycles.

Though it isn’t quite as impressive as our top picks for best overall and best high-capacity, the Jackery Explorer 300 v2 is compact, light, and a decent amount of power for its price. Less a mobile power station than an upscale power bank, the 8.16-pound Explorer 300 v2 handles device charging when you’re camping, on a job site, driving, or just need some power away from an outlet. Its 288Wh capacity isn’t huge, but it’s enough to keep phones, cameras and a laptop topped off, or run a small fan or light for a few hours. The 300W inverter (600W surge) won’t run a coffee maker, but it has a 100W USB-C port, and Jackery says a wall outlet refills it in about 76 minutes.

We tested the original Explorer 300, the portable power station this one replaces, for several months, and it came in handy numerous times, especially during the winter when power outages abound. At one point, we had it powering two phones, a MacBook, and a small light. We haven’t tested the v2 yet, but it’s in the same size class with a longer-lived battery: Jackery rates its LiFePO4 cells for 4,000 cycles before they drop to 70 percent of their original capacity.

Our original review unit got banged around in car trunks, duffel bags, and other less-than-luxurious accommodations with no issues. If you catch one of these on sale, get it and stick it in a cabinet. You’ll be extremely glad to have it around when the need arises.

Over the past few years, solar generators have exploded onto the market. There are now dozens of different brands that largely look more or less the same at a glance. The fact is, there are only a few standouts among a sea of knockoffs. Here’s what to look for to ensure you’re getting a great one:

A portable solar generator comes in a wide range of sizes, but a generator’s size doesn’t automatically make it capable of storing a lot of power. In fact, most are disappointingly limited and unable to store much more juice than a portable charger.

To properly check a generator’s storage, you must look at its capacity, measured in watt-hours (Wh). One watt-hour is the equivalent of 1 watt flowing over the course of an hour. The best solar generators offer capacities of several hundred and sometimes several thousand watt-hours. That doesn’t mean, however, that it will provide power for several hundred or several thousand hours. Any generator will ultimately last a different amount of time, depending on what’s plugged into it.

It’s easy to predict how long a generator will last when you use it to power one thing. For example, if you were to power a 100-watt bulb using a power station with a capacity of 500 watt-hours, it would stay lit for five continuous hours. Add a portable fridge with a 50W average draw, a phone charger drawing up to 18W, a 3W mini-fan, and runtime drops accordingly. The more capacity, the better.

No solar generator will hold a charge forever, so you want one capable of charging as quickly and easily as possible. This is where we put the “renewable” into “renewable energy.”

All of the power stations included in this roundup can be charged by connecting them to solar panels (hence the designation “solar generators”). Still, you also want to look for the ability to charge via other sources like wall outlets and your vehicle’s 12-volt plug. This ensures that you can charge up whether you’re off-grid in the sun, plugged in while preparing at home, or using your dash socket on the go.

You must also monitor a model’s charging input capacity, measured in watts (W). For example, a solar-powered generator with a max input of 100W can take in a continuous flow of up to 100 watts, which is about the minimum that you’ll reasonably want to look for. Most of the generators below have input capacities of at least a few hundred watts when charging via solar, so a few 50- to 200-watt solar panels will max them out.

Solar generators need to keep the power coming in and going out. The best solar generators can simultaneously charge all your intended devices via whatever plugs are necessary.

Any portable power station worth your money will have a high output capacity so you can charge many devices, even if they require a lot of juice. At a minimum, you’ll want a generator that can put out 300 watts at a time, though you’ll want at least 500 for larger tasks.

The best solar generators should also offer a variety of output plugs, including AC outlets, USB-A, USB-C, and even 12-volt DC outlets like the one in your vehicle dash. This ensures you can charge several devices simultaneously regardless of their plug. The number of ports you’ll need will vary depending on how many devices you need to power, but it should have at least a couple of AC outlets and enough USB-C and USB-A ports, at suitable wattages, for your devices.

While portable battery sources have been around for a while now, over the past several decades, they’ve been pretty heavy, unwieldy things. One of the most exciting aspects of the latest generation of solar generators is that they’ve become much more physically compact.

Suppose you plan on taking a generator camping or working it into a van conversion where every square inch matters; well, size and weight become major considerations. All of the products we’ve recommended are about the size of one or two shoeboxes, three at the most. The lightest weighs about 7 pounds, while the heaviest standalone unit is about 84 pounds. Most fall somewhere between 30 and 60 pounds.

If you’re using your generator as a more or less stationary source of backup power at home, portability isn’t a huge issue. Still, we generally recommend keeping weight and size in mind; you never know when you’ll need it for something other than a backup. (Plus, who wants to lug around something heavy and awkward if they don’t have to?)

Another consideration regarding portability involves the necessity for accessories, which can impact how easy it is to move and use your generator. Some generators, for example, require a lot of removable battery packs, which can be a hassle when you’re on the go or packing a vehicle. All of the picks on our list work on their own, though solar charging requires compatible panels and cables.

As with any product you expect to last, durability and all-around quality craftsmanship are essential. This is especially true if you plan on lugging your generator around on camping and road trips. Many subpar power stations are made from cheap components and flimsy plastic that doesn’t feel like it will hold up under the rigors of the road.

Durability isn’t something you can determine by reading a spec sheet off the internet. You’ve actually got to take the generator out, use it a bunch, and see how it holds up. I’ve verified the durability of these recommendations via a combination of my own actual field tests and reviews culled from countless real product owners. The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2, Explorer 1000 v2 and Explorer 300 v2 are the exceptions; we haven’t tested them yet.

It’s easy to underestimate how much capacity you need. 1,000 watt-hours might sound like a lot, but if you’re going to power a converted van with a portable fridge, lights, and occasional phone and laptop top-off, that 1,000 watt-hours will go faster than you expect. I used a setup like this and know from personal experience that you should always overestimate how much power you’ll need.A generator with a capacity under 1,000Wh can keep electronics charged. A larger one with 1,000 to 1,500Wh should be the minimum for road trips where you’ll need it to last multiple days between full charges. For a house or worksite where you expect to use some serious energy, like a full-sized refrigerator or power tools, you’re going to want to start looking at the biggest possible power stations that can be daisy-chained to external batteries.If you want to get precise, there is an equation:1. Estimate how many hours you’ll need to power various devices. For example, if you want to power two light bulbs for two hours, you need two hours of operation.2. Add up the total wattage necessary: the two bulbs are 60 watts each, so you need 120 watts.3. Multiply these together to find the total watt-hours needed: 2 x 120 = 240Wh. Leave room for conversion losses and a reserve, and you’d want at least a 300Wh solar generator. That might sound like a lot for two lightbulbs, but remember that, in most situations, you won’t really be powering 60-watt light bulbs for hours on end. You’ll be charging phones and laptops for an hour here or there, cooling a fridge that kicks on and off every once in a while, using power tools in short bursts, and whatnot.

Power stations are rated in charge cycles, not years. Jackery rates its v2 Explorers for 4,000 cycles before they drop to 70 percent of their original capacity, for example. How many years that adds up to depends on how often you drain and refill the battery, and on storing it within the manufacturer’s temperature range. The best-designed power stations are pretty sturdy, with few to no moving parts, so they should likely keep kicking for a long time, provided that you care for them properly. I’ve been pretty rough with a few of mine, and they show no signs of stopping.

Yes and no. While it’s absolutely possible to power your house with solar power, you’re unlikely to do so with a portable solar generator unless you use several at once while limiting your power usage. High-capacity picks such as the Bluetti Apex 300 and EcoFlow Delta 3 Ultra Plus come closest when paired with extra batteries, but how long they last depends on what you run, how much solar you can add, and the weather. Running house circuits, rather than plugging appliances straight into the station, requires a transfer switch or interlock installed by an electrician. Never backfeed power through a wall outlet.

We’re living in a “golden age” for portable solar generators. When I was a kid, and my family was playing around with solar gear while camping in the ‘90s, the technology couldn’t charge many devices, so it wasn’t all that practical.

By contrast, the solar generators I’ve recommended here are incredibly useful. I’ve relied on them to power my work and day-to-day needs while road-tripping nationwide. They’re also great when the power goes out. When a windstorm cut the power at my house for a couple of days, I was still working, watching my stories, and keeping the lights on.

We haven’t even scratched the surface in terms of the potential offered by portable, reliable, renewable, relatively affordable power. What we can do now is already incredible. The potential for what may come next, though, is even more exciting.

We replaced two picks that went out of stock or out of production with the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 and Jackery Explorer 1000 v2, swapped the original Jackery Explorer 300 for the current Explorer 300 v2, removed the Anker 767, Goal Zero Yeti 1000 Core, EcoFlow Delta 2 Max and DJI Power 2000, corrected the Bluetti Apex 300’s specs to match the standalone unit, updated prices, and re-checked every pick on November 4, 2026.

#4629. Xiaomi’s humanoid robots work a full 8-hour shift in its EV factory

Xiaomi has released footage of its humanoid robots working a full 8-hour shift at its EV factory, sorting center console side covers for its cars. The company says the robots did it on their own, catching and fixing their own mistakes along the way.

If that’s fully autonomous, it’s truly impressive. But we’ve been disappointed by humanoid robot demos before, and Xiaomi left out the numbers that would let anyone check.

Xiaomi Tech posted the video on X on November 3, as the company picked up awards at the World Internet Conference in Wuzhen. It shows the robots pulling side covers from bins, carrying them to storage racks, and placing them into slots, with a running clock of cumulative working time and an “Autonomous, 100x Speed” label in the corner.

8 hours on the production line. 🤖Xiaomi’s full-size humanoid robot takes on an 8-hour task at the Center Console Side-Cover Sorting Workstation at Xiaomi Auto Factory.Beyond sustained operation, it can autonomously detect and correct anomalies while coordinating with the… pic.twitter.com/brpO3S5bCn

According to Xiaomi, the robot covered the full day of production needs at that workstation. The company says it detected and corrected anomalies on its own and coordinated with the production line’s control system, calling it “another step toward real-world industrial deployment.”

This is the third milestone in a program Xiaomi has been running in public all year. In March, it put a humanoid in its Beijing EV factory as an “intern” installing self-tapping nuts. Xiaomi reported a 90.2% success rate over three hours, fast enough to meet the station’s 76-second cycle time. By July, it said that success rate was up to 98%, and it added two harder stations, including the side-cover sorting job from this week’s video.

Last December, Xiaomi’s CEO, Lei Jun, said the company plans to deploy humanoid robots in large numbers across its factories within five years.

Xiaomi also announced that its open-source Xiaomi-Robotics-1 AI model, pre-trained on 100,000 hours of real-world robot data, has started trial runs in Xiaomi staff apartments. In a 30-minute run, it completed more than 50 task chains across three rooms.

Xiaomi didn’t say how many parts the robots sorted, what the success rate was over eight hours, or how many times a human had to step in. It also didn’t explain how the robots stayed powered for a full shift: swapped batteries, a tether, or charging breaks.

And that matters, because “autonomous” in a robot video can mean anything. Tesla’s Optimus robots at the 2024 “We, Robot” event were remotely operated by humans, which Tesla didn’t disclose at the time. Last December, an Optimus took a suspicious tumble in a Miami demo, raising its hands to its head like a teleoperator pulling off a VR headset as it fell.

To be fair to Xiaomi, it has published success rates and cycle times for its earlier factory tests. That’s more than Tesla has ever shared about Optimus doing useful work, and Tesla now says it won’t deliver Optimus to outside customers until late 2027.

The most interesting moment in the video comes around the 1:37 mark. In a segment Xiaomi labels “Dropped Material: Multi-Robot Collaboration,” a humanoid upper body mounted on a wheeled base rolls in to help the two legged robots.

It’s not the only thing on wheels in that scene, either. The bins of parts are shuttled around by autonomous mobile robots, the same kind of wheeled platforms that have been moving materials in car factories for years.

They could have got a lot more done if they'd moved the parts bins closer so the bots didn't have to walk as far. That's a huge open space between the two.

If this demo was truly fully autonomous for eight hours, with the robots handling their own errors, that’s one of the more impressive humanoid demos we’ve seen. Xiaomi deserves credit for putting its robots on a real production line and publishing some real numbers along the way. But we’ve been burned by “autonomous” robot demos before, so we’ll wait for more details before getting too excited.

The wheeled robot is our favorite part of the video, though. It’s a great example of why you shouldn’t bet everything on the humanoid form factor. Wheels are far more efficient than legs on most terrain, and a flat factory floor is the best-case scenario for wheels. A wheeled base doesn’t burn energy just to stay upright, it’s more stable when carrying parts, it has room for a much bigger battery (which would solve that 8-hour power question), and it needs fewer expensive actuators.

The value in these robots is in the hands, arms, and the AI driving them. Legs make sense in homes with stairs, and maybe that’s where Xiaomi wants to take them eventually. But factories were designed around carts and forklifts, not people walking around carrying parts.

As robots and AI put more strain on the grid and electricity rates climb, solar and batteries are becoming essential home infrastructure, not a luxury. #4628. The 2027 Mercedes-AMG GT 63 4-Door Coupe Turns a New Page for AMG

An EV that sounds, and often feels, like it has been inspired by AMG’s V-8-powered past.

The 2027 Mercedes-AMG GT 63 4-Door Coupe marks an entirely new era for AMG. There isn’t a lick of hardware shared between this electric performance sedan and the milquetoast AMG EVs that came before it. The same goes for its drive software, which is as equally important as the exotic electric powertrain hiding under the car’s polarizing metal and LEDs. More than anything, this car is a statement to the world that Mercedes and AMG mean business in the cutthroat world of rapidly evolving electric performance.

It is familiar to AMG’s combustion offerings on purpose. Twist the dial over to Sport+ on the steering wheel, and the most convincing engine and transmission simulation in an EV yet comes to life. There’s no blend between electric motor and gasoline sounds to be heard here. It’s the twin-turbo 4.0-liter V-8 from the previous-generation AMG GT R Coupe, and it’s quite the circus act.

Mercedes calls it AMGFORCE Sport+ (a terrible name), and engineers took over 100 measurements with 16 microphone positions that allowed software gurus to reconstruct the sound digitally. What makes it convincing isn’t the sound, though. Mercedes uses the Burmester 4D sound exciters in the seats that produce vibrations with music to replicate the vibration and harshness you’d feel if a real V-8 were running up and down its rev range. You have to surrender your brain to the simulation, but if you do, it works. I was cackling in the driver’s seat all day, but you can just as easily turn off the fun and games for a pure EV soundscape.

Like other systems that do the same (see the Hyundai Ioniq 5 and the Genesis GV60), the AMG multiclutch transmission is fully simulated too. With a “redline” at 7200 rpm, the car lets you manually shift through seven speeds via steering-wheel-mounted paddles. Downshifts are accompanied with realistic engine braking on the overrun. Sadly, you can’t bang it off a simulated rev limiter at the top of each “gear,” but it’s still a hoot. If there’s a downside to this system, it’s the fake noise being piped to the outside world. Similar to Dodge’s cringey Fratzonic exhaust, Mercedes uses an exterior speaker system to project V-8 sounds from the rear of the car. Once the myth is busted, this is not convincing anybody and is likely to make a driver the butt of many a joke at the local Cars & Coffee.

V-8 clone technology aside, the AMG GT 63 4-Door Coupe produces numbers that should make even the staunchest of doubters raise an eyebrow in interest. Three axial flux motors—two in the rear and one in front—engineered with YASA combine to produce 1153 hp and 1475 lb-ft of torque. That peak power is accomplished in either Race or Boost mode, but don’t fret about it being temporary. Boost mode lasts a wild 63 seconds should you want it, and AMG says it could truly continue for as long as you desire in Race with zero derating. Standard, continuous output in other modes sits at 711 hp.

My first drive was at the gorgeous Ascari racetrack in southern Spain. It’s the ideal place to test out the car’s claimed 0–60-mph time of 2.3 seconds, and while I didn’t come close to the electronically limited 186-mph top speed, its rapid pull up to and beyond 130 mph suggests the limiter won’t take too long to reach.

There are several keys to this big sedan’s ability to run lap after lap at the track. One is direct oil cooling for the motors and gearsets, this using a proprietary, secret oil. Next, Mercedes uses water-cooled silicon carbide inverters. And finally, the most important piece is the 106-kWh, 800-volt AMG High Performance Electric Battery. This battery pack was developed specifically for AMG models (it won’t be used elsewhere) and uses unique cells with electrically nonconducting cooling oil flowing around each one.

The thermal management going on here is second to none, and on top of the track performance, it enables DC fast-charging at speeds beyond 600 kilowatts. That’s faster than any other EV on sale in America today. No, there aren’t any charging stations in the U.S. to support that madness, but Mercedes wheeled out a charger for a demonstration at Ascari, and I witnessed speeds of over 630 kilowatts. The claim is 10–80 percent in only 11 minutes, and given the right charger, this car can make that happen.

Lots of power doesn’t necessarily make a great EV, but that’s where AMG’s software wizards come into play. This tri-motor setup is truly only as competent as the software that’s running it, because there isn’t a single center differential or torque-vectoring diff to be found. Mercedes installed three completely independent electric motors with an absurd amount of torque and then went about making that controllable. Engineers tell me repeatedly that among the challenges, dialing in the proper drive characteristics was the biggest of all.

Funnily enough, this newfound flexibility in the powertrain led AMG to develop a set of dials with nine settings each it calls “AMG Race Engineer.” The Response Control dial lets you change throttle sensitivity, ranging from entirely dull to jumpy on the high end. A Traction Control dial does exactly what you’d expect, with one ensuring the car won’t slip an inch and nine turning the car into a full-on drift machine—there’s a Drift mode that shuts off the front motor too. Last, and most intriguing, there’s Agility Control. In practice, it’s like having an infinitely adjustable yaw controller at your beck and call. At one, it’s all understeer as you brake and steer into a corner. Dial it up to around the five-to-seven range, and the AMG transforms into a car with shockingly neutral balance, letting me induce just enough oversteer to coax the rear into a corner as I trail it in. Go all the way to nine, and you better watch yourself with how much the rear is going to be moving.

I’ve never driven a car that can behave so differently from corner to corner simply at the twist of a dial, but that’s the kind of freedom afforded by three extremely powerful, independent electric motors. When asked how the magic happens, engineers rattle on about how they’ve simulated differentials just by using positive and negative motor torque. Sometimes the car will be using brake regeneration at specific corners to induce the behavior you’ve selected; other times traditional brake torque vectoring intrudes to pinch the calipers to control the car’s movements. It all sounds like an impossible orchestra to compose, and yet somehow, they nailed it. All the way down to the adjustable traction control that lets you choose just how sideways you want to get accelerating out of a corner. Lock it down for safety, or send plumes of smoke into the air. The choice is genuinely entirely yours.

After a few laps of getting acclimated to how all these systems interact, I started to understand this big four-door’s personality. Around a racetrack, it drives similar to a Porsche Taycan that doesn’t take life so seriously. Or in other words, it drives how you’d expect an AMG product to, safely sliding around and roaring its V-8 trumpet.

The 63 comes with AMG’s Ride Control air suspension with active roll stabilization that uses the same hydraulically interconnected dampers as you’d find on the AMG GT 63 Coupe, allowing chassis engineers to delete the anti-roll bars. I didn’t drive the 63 on the road, but the ride over curbing was considerably better than I expected from a 5534-pound performance sedan that corners as flat as it does. Active aero in the form of underbody Venturi flow elements, a deployable rear spoiler, an extendable rear diffuser, and front cooling louvers keep the car in either the most advantageous aerodynamic profile for range or in maximum-downforce-and-stability mode.

The brakes are mighty, with carbon-ceramic rotors up front and steel rotors in the rear. Huge recuperation capability from the axial-flux electric motors means they don’t even have to work very hard. Despite eight laps around Ascari, there was hardly a whiff of brake smell when I pulled back into pit lane—yet another shock for a large and heavy EV. Unfortunately, brake feel is a sore point, with the pedal offering an airy sensation through the first half before firming up toward the bottom of the stroke. Braking distances seem comparable to other large performance sedans in practice, in part due to the Michelin Pilot Sport S 5 tires Mercedes fits. More aggressive Cup 2 tires would take this car to another level, but it’s a step engineers were hesitant to take with this model, perhaps saving the grippier rubber for a more extreme version to come.

My other biggest gripe: The fake V-8 and transmission disappear in Race mode. Outside of Sport+, this EV accelerates and sounds like any other megaquick electric car. It’s unending, brutal, and, eventually, a bit boring. Thankfully, the slidetastic chassis keeps things entertaining on the racetrack, though I suspect the number of owners who bring this beast to the track will be in the double digits at best. You can technically bring it there and pound around with none of the typical downsides of pushing an EV, but this AMG is no track star.

The AMG GT 63 4-Door Coupe starts at $176,500, which sure sounds high, but at the same time reasonable with how much effort AMG put into this car from a hardware, software, and material perspective. It’s also right in line with a Porsche Taycan Turbo, the GT 63’s closest competitor.

If you’re inclined to such an experience in an EV, there’s no better internal-combustion simulator in existence. Combine this party trick with the infinitely adjustable handling attitude, and you’re left looking at a technological fortress of performance. It’s one hell of a statement. I’m just not sure many people are going to be willing to listen to it.

Sony wants you to USB-C its new retro Walkman headphones. Now, more than a decade after the “Star-Lord headphones” introduced a new generation to the magic of the mixtape and the wonder of wired listening, and 10 years since Stranger Things debuted (and eventually featured a curse-breaking cassette), Sony has gone back to the 1979 hand-drawn drawings to revive the MDR-3L2 design for the plug-and-playlist era.

The new MDR-3R comes with blue and orange interchangeable earpads (shown at the top and bottom of the page), a nod to nostalgia with an extra option for expression. #4626. BYD’s new luxury electric SUV has one big problem: It weighs over 8,200 lbs

BYD’s new full-size electric SUV, the Denza N9 EV, was revealed in a regulatory filing, weighing in at over 8,200 lbs (3,760 kg). That creates one issue.

The Denza N9 first went on sale last March, a flagship plug-in hybrid (PHEV) SUV with a combined CLTC range of about 807 miles (1,300 km) on a full charge and full tank of gas.

BYD introduced the updated Flash Charging version earlier this year, which uses its second-generation Blade Batteries and delivers a pure electric CLTC range of 260 miles (420 km). Combined, it gets up to 944 miles (1,520 km) under CLTC conditions.

In the latest batch of new energy vehicles (NEVs) approved for sale by China’s MIIT (Ministry of Information Technology) this week, a new all-electric Denza N9 appeared.

The filing revealed the Denza N9 EV will be available with three electric motors, delivering a combined output of 1,193 horsepower (890 kW).

A badge on the back reveals it will use BYD’s tri-motor e3 platform. The setup features a single 362 horsepower (270 kW) front motor and two 415 horsepower (310 kW) rear electric motors.

The electric version measures 5,270 mm long, 2,030 mm wide, and 1,830 mm tall, with a 3,125 mm wheelbase, which is the same as the current Denza N9 PHEV Flash Charging model. It will be available in five- and six-seat configurations.

While the filing reveals it will use a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery with cells from BYD’s battery unit, FinDreams, it does not provide specifics like capacity or driving range.

One relatively big thing to note: the Denza N9 EV has a gross weight of 3,760 kg, or about 8,289 lbs.

Obscene weight , and that applies to other SUVs as well. Vehicle registration taxes should be based on vehicle weight as it wears out roads and endangers other road users and infrastructure and wastes resources.

As AutoNext points out, this makes it too heavy for an EU category B driving license, which covers up to 3,500 kg (7,716 lbs).

Last year, the EU updated the rules, allowing drivers who have held a category B license for two years to drive alternative-fuelled vehicles with a maximum weight of up to 4,250 kg (9,369 lbs).

While the Denza N9 EV would qualify as listed, newer drivers would still need a commercial EU category C1 driving license to drive it.

BYD launched its luxury sub-brand, Denza, in Europe and the UK in March, starting with the Z9 GT and the D9 van. More recently, it introduced the Bao 5 PHEV SUV and the Denza Z electric supercar.

#4625. Tokyo police consider using AI to reconstruct traffic accidents

Published Nov 5, 2026 11:07 AM EST

One law enforcement agency in Japan reportedly wants to make something normally confined to sci-fi crime thrillers a reality: interactive, AI-powered reconstructions of real-world accidents. According to The Japan Times, Tokyo’s Metropolitan Department is developing a system that combines AI with security camera footage and 3D spatial data captured by camera-equipped mapping vehicles to digitally reconstruct traffic accidents. Investigators using the tool would reportedly be able to measure vehicle speeds and distances on a screen and replay the event in simulation from multiple perspectives, including overhead or even through the eyes of a nearby driver or pedestrian.

That’s the goal, at least. Details about how this proposed system will actually work remain sparse, though the report says that the police plan to begin testing in June 2027 and potentially launch full operations in January 2028. In theory, digital reconstructions could reduce the need for labor-intensive physical, on-site inspections (the current approach) which can close off roads for ours and lead to traffic jams.

However, AI reconstructions bring risks of their own, especially if they rely on generative AI tools that are prone to hallucinating fabricated data. In the United States  and elsewhere, courts are struggling to reign in examples of inaccurate, AI-generated court filings and police reports. The use of AI-enhanced video and audio and even deepfake clones presented in trials are also forcing the legal system to reevaluate how it treats algorithm-altered evidence.

As far as we can tell, the Tokyo police proposal would be the first systematic use of an AI reconstruction for traffic assessments. In 2024, law enforcement in Pune, India, east of Mumbai, reportedly considered using an AI-enabled “digital reconstruction” to analyze a high profile drunk driving incident that killed two pedestrians. But it’s unclear whether that system was ever actually realized or used in court.

Researchers have been exploring the underlying technology for such a system for years. In July, a team from the Technical University of Munich and the Bavarian State Criminal Police Office in Germany showed off an AI system they say is capable of compiling thousands of photographers from a crime scene to create a digital reconstruction. In that case, the team said the system could automatically identify and classify objects in the scene. Investigators could then virtually go in and query the 3D crime scene to try and collect and analyze evidence long after the actual event occurred.

Meanwhile, researchers at Hasselt University in Belgium, are also in the early stage of developing a tool aiming to use multimodal language models for digital reconstructions which they say could aid law enforcement and insurers.

Generative AI tools are also creating new headaches for the legal system. Hundreds of lawyers around the globe have been sanctioned by courts for filling legal briefs with bogus, hallucinated case law. In June, a judge in Mississippi canceled a civil trial’s proceedings after all four lawyers on opposing sides of the case were caught citing a fake, AI-generated court filing. And citations are not the only issue. A growing number of police departments in the U.S. are using AI tools to analyze evidence and draft police reports, which the American Civil Liberty Union warns “removes important human elements from police procedures.”

At least partially AI-generated evidence, like the kind that many result from a digital reconstitution, has already appeared in some legal proceedings. In 2024, a Washington State judge overseeing a murder case barred the defendant’s lawyers from introducing cellphone footage that had been digitally enhanced using AI software. According to court filings at the time, the judge in that case worried that admitting that AI- enhanced footage could “lead to a confusion of the issue and muddling of eyewitness testimony.”

The core tension here, and with other uses of AI as evidence, is whether or not the AI system can be trusted to accurately reflect reality. An AI system reconstructing traffic scenes, though potentially  less higher stages than a murder trial, may nonetheless face similar headwinds.

#4624. Florida Man Who Allegedly Stole $210,000 Porsche Panamera Apparently Forgot He Was Wearing a GPS Ankle Monitor

A previous police chase had earned the 19-year-old suspect a tracking device, which investigators say placed him at the scene of the Porsche theft.

We at Road & Track certainly don't know if a handbook for car thieves exists. But if it did, there would certainly have to be a chapter on how to avoid getting caught. And that chapter probably begins with some fairly obvious advice—like, for example, don't steal a $210,000 Porsche Panamera while wearing a GPS ankle monitor that tells the authorities exactly where you are.

According to a report by WPLG Local 10 News, 19-year-old Joseph Dexter Watson IV has been accused by authorities of participating in the October 24 theft of a Porsche Panamera. The luxury car was reportedly stolen from a multimillion-dollar mansion in Miami-Dade County's Horse Country neighborhood.

According to investigators, Watson and at least three accomplices arrived at the property in a Mercedes-Benz shortly before 6:30 p.m. The group allegedly broke into a Cadillac Escalade parked outside the gated property, but apparently not satisfied with the score, one of the suspects reportedly climbed over a fence and stole the Porsche. Inside the Panamera, authorities say, were seven pairs of shoes valued at roughly $4200. The Porsche's owner quickly tracked the car to a Hampton Inn parking lot in Deerfield Beach; When Broward Sheriff's Office deputies arrived, they found the Porsche, but nobody was inside.

However, locating one of the suspects was surprisingly easy. See, in January, Watson allegedly led police on a bizarre chase: according to authorities, the rented Kia he was driving crashed into a mail truck, when he then reportedly tried to hide in another mail truck before attempting to flee the scene in an Uber. Watson was caught and spent approximately two months in jail before being released on bond in March.

As a condition of his release, Watson was ordered to wear a GPS ankle monitor. According to investigators, it was that very monitor that placed him at the scene of the Porsche theft. He now faces new charges, including traveling with intent to commit burglary of an occupied dwelling, masked burglary of an occupied dwelling, and grand theft of a motor vehicle. He is being held at the Turner Guilford Knight Correctional Center—this time, without bond.

#4622. Germany’s EV share hits record 37% as BEVs beat gas and diesel combined

Battery-electric cars took a record 37% of Germany’s new car market in October, according to data released today by the Kraftfahrt-Bundesamt (KBA), the country’s federal motor vehicle authority. That’s 94,086 BEVs, up 79.5% from 52,425 a year earlier.

For the second month in a row, German buyers registered more fully electric cars than gasoline and diesel cars combined. And with two months left in the year, Germany has already blown past the auto industry’s EV forecast for all of 2026.

The overall market barely grew in October. Total new car registrations rose 1.7% to 254,492 units, which means the EV growth came straight out of combustion cars.

Gasoline car registrations crashed 40.5% to 38,516 units, a 15.1% share. Diesel fell 21.6% to 23,882 units, or 9.4% of the market. Add them up and pure combustion cars made up just 24.5% of new registrations, 12.5 points less than BEVs alone.

Plug-in hybrids slipped 7.9% to 28,499 units (11.2%). So plug-ins accounted for about 48% of the German market last month, and the average CO2 emissions of new cars dropped 21.1% year-over-year to 79.4 g/km.

As we reported this summer, BEVs became the most popular powertrain in Germany for the first time in June with a 28.4% share. They’ve kept climbing every month since: 32.4% in August, 34.5% in September, and now 37% in October.

Through the first ten months of the year, Germany has registered 698,230 BEVs, up 60.7% year-over-year. That’s about 28.2% of the 2,476,290 new cars registered in 2026 so far, up from roughly 19% for the full year 2025.

And the industry didn’t see it coming. In December, the VDA, Germany’s auto industry association, forecast about 693,000 BEV registrations for all of 2026. Germany passed that in October. At the current pace, it’s on track for somewhere around 875,000 by the end of the year.

The biggest driver is Germany’s new EV incentive, which applies retroactively to cars registered since January 1. It pays €3,000 for a new BEV, bought or leased, and up to €6,000 for lower-income households with children. Households with taxable income above €80,000 (€90,000 with kids) don’t qualify.

The program targets private buyers, and that’s exactly where the KBA data shows the jump. Private registrations rose 20.6% in October, while commercial registrations fell 8.2%. Private buyers now make up 40.7% of the market.

Germany has been here before. The government killed its previous EV incentive overnight in December 2023, and BEV sales fell off a cliff in 2024. This time, the money is going to the buyers who need it most, and it’s moving the needle fast.

Tesla’s German numbers swing wildly with its quarterly delivery cycle. In September, the end of the quarter, it registered 12,552 cars (+268.7%) and the Model Y was the best-selling car in Germany. In October, it registered only 2,932, which is still up 290.9% but from a tiny base, for a 1.2% market share.

Year-to-date, Tesla is up 206.1% to 47,742 registrations. That’s a big rebound from a terrible 2025, but BYD is now slightly ahead with 47,961 (+216.1%). BYD registered 5,173 cars in October (+54.3%), though the majority of its German sales are plug-in hybrids, not BEVs.

The other Chinese brands are growing even faster. Leapmotor registered 3,661 cars in October, up 288.6%, and is at 19,705 for the year. Xpeng was up 284.4% to 1,380 units, and SAIC’s MG was up 48.5% to 4,140.

Volkswagen Group still owns the top of the EV charts, though. Through September, the Skoda Elroq was Germany’s best-selling EV with 30,845 units, ahead of the Tesla Model Y (29,464) and the VW ID.3 (24,352).

The EV boom is happening during one of the worst years in the history of Germany’s auto industry.

In October, the VW brand’s German registrations fell 4%, Audi dropped 8.4%, Porsche lost 5.7%, and Opel crashed 24.1%. BMW was flat (+0.1%), and Mercedes was the exception, up 8.5%. VW is still by far the biggest brand in Germany with an 18.2% share, but it’s down 5.6% for the year.

Last week, Volkswagen Group reported a €5.9 billion operating loss for the third quarter, its biggest quarterly loss since Dieselgate, driven by a writedown of its Porsche stake, weak sales in China, and thin EV margins. The group has already approved a plan to cut 100,000 jobs and close several German plants. Mercedes cut its 2026 car margin guidance to 2-3% last week, mainly because of China.

It’s not a product problem. VW’s new ID. Polo is sold out with over 30,000 orders, BMW has over 50,000 orders for the Neue Klasse iX3, and the Elroq leads the German EV market.

Germany is proving what we’ve been saying for years. Give buyers EVs they can actually afford, and they switch fast. Fully electric cars went from about 19% of the market last year to 37% in October, and the country beat the industry’s full-year forecast with two months to spare. That’s not a slow transition.

One thing to consider when talking about EVs not being Germany-made is that Germany car makers can't make them fast enough. A lot of the models are sold out for months. It's not an excuse but something to keep in mind.

Compare that with North America, where EV sales dropped 44% after the US killed its federal EV tax credit. Same technology, sometimes the same cars. The difference is policy.

Germany’s problem is who’s capturing the demand. Hint: it’s not German automakers.

But whose fault is that? You can’t spend years dragging your feet on electrification and lobby government back and forth on EV incentives and then complain when those who are all-in on EVs are able to take better advantage of the customer shift amid another oil crisis.

If you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero. #4621. 1,500 years ago, a man trekked across Europe as the Roman Empire fell

Published Nov 5, 2026 11:56 AM EST

If you were going to live in Europe at any point in time, word of advice: Avoid the fifth century. The mighty Roman Empire was floundering. Attila the Hun repeatedly invaded the eastern Roman Empire, and even Italy in the year 452 CE. Fierce Germanic forces known as the Visigoths and Vandals sacked and raided Rome, first in 410 and again in 455. The Franks (in present-day France, Belgium, and western Germany) were busy wresting control in the west. And in 476, the entire Roman Empire collapsed. Put simply, it was a rough century.

With all of that upheaval, many people picked up and left their homes, undoubtedly in search of better, more stable places to live. Historians call the period between the fourth and seventh centuries in Europe as the Migration Period since so many people were on the move.

Now, thanks to some 1,500-year-old DNA from an elaborate ship burial in northwestern Germany, we are tantalizingly close to understanding one man’s journey from one end of the Roman Empire to the other. Oh, and he also had leprosy.

This grueling, potentially 800-mile-long journey is detailed in a study published in this month’s edition of the journal iScience.

Discovered in the 1990s, the Fallward burial ground is a treasure trove of information from the Migration Period. Located on coastal marshland, about 20 miles west of Hamburg, Germany, the cemetery contains about 200 cremation burials and 60 graves from the end of the third to the late fifth century. Many of the graves were dug deep into damp clay, which has helped preserve many striking finds.

One of the most remarkable graves is simply labeled as site 265. The grave belongs to an approximately 50-year-old man, who died sometime between 425 and 450. The man probably rowed or fished along the German coast since his skeletal remains indicate his upper arm muscles were well developed. He was also buried inside a 13-foot-long oak boat covered with wooden panels that formed a roof-like structure.

But the boat burial isn’t the only thing that makes grave 265 unique.

“The grave goods placed in the tomb aroused particular scientific interest; these included a chair, artfully decorated and carved from an alder trunk. Furthermore, the man possessed a late Roman military belt, which suggested that the deceased had had connections across great distances,” explained Dr. Hauke Jöns from the Lower Saxony Institute for Historical Coastal Research in Wilhelmshaven, Germany, explained in a statement on the new findings.

The elaborate chair was presumably painted and is often referred to as a throne. Far from an ordinary piece of furniture meant for daily use, it was instead a symbol of the authority the deceased wielded in life.

The late Roman military belt perhaps raises the most questions about who the man buried in 265 was. The belt shows signs of both use and repair. While its presence doesn’t necessarily mean the man was a soldier in the Roman military—he could’ve acquired it through trade, inheritance, or as war booty—it also doesn’t mean he wasn’t a soldier for Rome. If he was, he would have likely been part of the foederati. These warriors served Rome through a treaty, or foedus, rather than as Roman citizens.

The grave also included: a stool carved with a hunting scene and inscription, a game board, a ceramic vessel, and a bronze basin.

For nearly 30 years, archaeologists could only speculate about what these grave goods meant about who was buried in grave 265. But with the new DNA analysis, we now have some concrete answers about who this man was. Though the team was able to extract DNA from three individuals from the Fallward burial ground, “the results were particularly striking” for the man in 265. The new genetic analysis confirms two things about the man.

First, he was from or had close family from the Danube region in the eastern part of the Roman Empire, which comprised parts of modern day Croatia, Hungary, Slovenia, and Serbia. That’s a long way from his grave in northwestern Germany, so at some point he or a close relative traveled more than 800 miles, leaving behind the Roman Empire in process. Second, he had a rare form of leprosy.

“Leprosy is a chronic disease. It can take years for clear symptoms to appear. The man had not yet suffered any bone damage. Either he was affected by an asymptomatic form of the disease, or the disease had so far only affected soft tissues. He may have travelled long distances whilst carrying the disease,” explained study co-author Dr. Almut Nebel from the Institute of Clinical Molecular Biology (IKMB) at Christian-Albrechts-University in Kiel, Germany.

Study co-author Dr. Ben Krause-Kyora (also at IKMB) speculates, “He could, for example, have been a mercenary in the Roman army who later settled between the Elbe and the Weser [rivers, which run on either side of Fallward]. Or he might have undertaken long journeys as a trader.”

Either way, the man in grave 265 likely lived through a heck of a lot before taking up fishing on the rural German coastline.

#4620. The Toyota Supra and BMW Z4 Are Officially Sold Out: Report

Production for the sibling sports car pair has ended, and the last units in the U.S. have, apparently, left dealer lots.

When BMW and Toyota first joined forces to reimagine two iconic sports car nameplates—the Supra and the Z4—the collaboration was a surprise, but also turned out to be quite a success, at least in terms of the smiles both cars delivered. Six years later, Toyota and BMW are sunsetting production of the sibling sports cars, and shoppers have apparently bought out all the remaining inventory.

National inventory data analyzed by CarsDirect brought to broader attention by Motor1 indicates that all new Toyota GR Supra and BMW Z4 units have been sold. (Road & Track found a handful of new Supra and Z4 listings on Autotrader, for what it’s worth, but that info is subject to dealers remembering to update their listings.) Both manufacturers ended production of the sports cars, which were built at the Magna Steyr factory in Austria, back in March.

Despite genuine enthusiast love, neither the GR Supra nor the Z4 sold particularly well. Toyota sold 2953 GR Supras in 2025, while BMW sold 2113 units of the Z4. All told, around 31,228 GR Supra units were sold in the U.S. since 2020. Similarly, BMW sold about 15,282 units of the fifth-generation Z4 in the U.S.

BMW offered a Z4 Final Edition in December 2025 with Individual Frozen Black Metallic paint and a Moonlight Black soft top. Toyota also offered a Final Edition GR Supra in May 2026, featuring larger brakes, adjusted suspension, and matte black paint. 1300 Final Edition GR Supra units made it to the U.S.

Toyota has not officially announced plans for a sixth-generation GR Supra, though company executives said the sports car will likely return. “It would be logical that we would have a next-gen Supra. But when and how is still TBD,” senior vice president of Product Planning and Strategy for Toyota Motor North America Cooper Ericksen said to MotorTrend.

BMW, however, has no current plans to bring a sixth-generation roadster to production. It remains unclear if BMW will bring another roadster to market.

A New York transplant hailing from the Pacific Northwest, Emmet White has a passion for anything that goes: cars, bicycles, planes, and motorcycles. After learning to ride at 17, Emmet worked in the motorcycle industry before joining Autoweek in 2022 and Road & Track in 2024. The woes of alternate side parking have kept his fleet moderate, with a 2014 Volkswagen Jetta GLI and a BMW 318i E30 street parked in his Queens community.

#4619. Range Rover is axing its two cheapest SUVs, making way for a new entry-level EV

Range Rover is pulling the plug on its two most affordable models, the Evoque and Velar, as a new entry-level EV steps in.

For decades, the Range Rover name was viewed as a status symbol, mostly used by wealthy buyers, high-powered executives, and even royalty.

That started to change with the launch of the Evoque in 2011 and the Velar in 2017, making the iconic British luxury brand a little more accessible.

In the US, the 2026 Range Rover Evoque starts at $49,900, and the Velar starts at $61,600. That’s considerably less than the Sport and flagship Range Rover SUVs, which start at $83,700 and $107,400, respectively.

Range Rover’s accessible luxury era is reportedly drawing to a close. Martin Limbert, Range Rover’s managing director, confirmed to Autocar that the Evoque and Velar will officially be discontinued, with production set to end in 2027.

While it has no direct replacement planned, the new Range Rover GT will serve as the brand’s new entry-level vehicle.

Range Rover revealed the GT in July, presenting it as the fifth and newest member of the lineup. Unlike the distinct SUV design Range Rover has built the brand on, the GT is a low-slung grand tourer.

The electric GT is “a captivating new expression” of the brand, Range said, describing it as “the most technologically sophisticated” model it’s ever designed.

It’s expected to be among the first vehicles based on JLR’s new EMA platform. Initially, the Range Rover GT will launch as a battery-electric vehicle (BEV), but Range Rover plans to add a full-hybrid (HEV) option later in the lifecycle.

Production of the Range Rover GT is set to begin in the first half of 2027 at JLR’s Halewood, UK plant, following the flagship electric SUV and smaller Sport EV model (shown below).

The Range Rover GT is expected to start at around $90,000 with an EPA range of at least 300 miles when it goes on sale as a 2028 model. In the UK, it will likely be over £75,000 ($100,000).

Range Rover’s flagship electric SUV starts at $140,450 in the US, and the smaller Sport EV will likely be a bit cheaper at around $120,000 to $130,000.

At $90,000, the electric GT isn’t what most would consider an “entry-level” vehicle, but it’s part of Range Rover’s push into higher-end, more profitable models.

#4617. 2026 Tesla Model Y Performance vs. 2027 Rivian R2 Performance Comparison Test

The R2 brings an intuitive, spacious cabin and a classy design, while the Model Y provides handling prowess and impressive near-self-driving capability.

“You come at the king, you best not miss.” That line, uttered menacingly by Michael K. Williams as Omar Little in The Wire, sums up the situation Rivian finds itself in as it launches the R2. The California-based startup broke onto the scene in 2021 with the excellent R1T pickup, and soon after the R1S SUV, but the R2, with its more affordable price point, is the product that could truly solidify Rivian’s place in the market.

To do that, though, Rivian is taking aim at the undisputed king of EVs, the Tesla Model Y, which is the bestselling EV in the United States. Rivian obviously doesn’t expect to overtake the Model Y on the sales charts overnight, but the R2 had better land at least a few punches, because a swing and a miss in the crucial compact SUV segment could see Rivian wind up like Fisker. To assess Rivian’s latest effort, we lined up a 2027 Rivian R2 Performance against a Tesla Model Y Performance in a battle of high-tech, superquick electric SUVs.

See all results for new 2027 Rivian R2 for sale near 60629

While Rivian plans to sell a $46,485 base model starting next year, the R2 launched for the 2027 model year exclusively in the punchy Performance trim. Initial versions come standard with the Launch package, which includes the hands-free driving assistance system and a 4400-pound tow package, which on later R2s will cost $2500 and $950, respectively. The example we drove had the standard setup of all-season tires wrapped around 21-inch wheels, with the only option, $2000 Launch Green paint, bringing the total to $61,485. The boxy newcomer faces off against an EV mainstay in the Model Y. The Performance model we tested had but one option, Full Self-Driving (Supervised), so we tacked on three years’ worth of the $99-per-month subscription, $3564, to come in at $63,194. Tesla fits the Model Y Performance with a trailer hitch as standard, and the sporty SUV can tow up to 3500 pounds.

The R2 and Model Y may be direct competitors, but they take on drastically different shapes. The Model Y features Tesla’s signature egg-like silhouette, and while lesser Model Ys are fairly anonymous looking, the Performance looks pretty sharp in Ultra Red paint with black wheels and trim. The Performance also sports a reshaped front bumper and a small rear lip spoiler.

The R2 is more rectangular, essentially looking like a shrunken version of the R1S. Rivian’s ovoid headlights are more distinctive and affable than the Tesla’s front light bar, which has the menacing look of the eyes on Iron Man’s mask. The R2’s front bumper, with an integrated silver skid plate and tow hooks, hints at the Rivian’s more outdoorsy aura.

The different vibes continue inside, despite both automakers heavily favoring screens over physical controls. In typical Tesla fashion, the Model Y’s interior feels bare, centered around the 16-inch touchscreen. The dashboard, door panels, and center console all have a simple, bland design, although ambient lighting injects a bit of pizzazz. The Performance model’s front seats get more substantial bolstering and a fun “warp speed” badge nestled in below the headrest. Build quality and materials quality have improved greatly since the Model Y’s early days, and carbon-fiber inserts imbue the Performance with a sporty feel. But the materials still aren’t as rich as those in the Rivian—Tesla’s vegan faux leather feels slightly plasticky, and the soft-touch surfaces aren’t as plush.

See all results for new 2027 Rivian R2 for sale near 60629

The R2 looks and feels far more upscale, with a more modern and purposeful design than the austere Tesla. The layered dashboard design is particularly rich: The synthetic leather upper feels like the real deal, tactile wood trim serves as a platform for the touchscreen, and a textured fabric resides below. Hard plastics are well hidden, confined to the lower reaches of the door panels and center console.

In the Tesla, nearly every function, from the climate controls to simply putting the car in drive, is done on the touchscreen, so it’s a relief that Tesla’s display is among the best in the game. The screen is responsive, with an easy-to-read interface. The number of tasks it handles and the amount of information it displays is overwhelming at first, but you quickly learn where the most important functions reside. Still, we prefer physical buttons for things like climate controls, drive modes, and regenerative-braking settings. Shifting between drive and reverse on a screen will always feel a bit odd, and sometimes the Model Y can even shift automatically without any driver input, which is both cool and a little freaky.

Tesla’s infotainment system is absolutely loaded with features, from a built-in dash cam to a web browser and arcade games to pass the time while charging. There’s even Zoom, should you need to pull over to take a meeting, and a Theater app that lets you stream shows and movies while parked. The Model Y also comes with Grok, Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence assistant, and the Toybox, which allows for shenanigans such as turning the seats into whoopee cushions, using the interior camera to transform the car into a photo booth and the exterior speakers to play silly sounds, or making the screen into a virtual sketchpad.

Rivian is also reliant on screens but takes a more traditional approach, complementing the 15.6-inch center touchscreen with an 11.5-inch digital gauge cluster. Rivian’s infotainment is clear and responsive, and the interface feels friendlier than Tesla’s slightly cold digital environment, with a furry, cheerful mascot for the Gear Guard security system and each drive mode accompanied by vivid illustrations. Neither Tesla nor Rivian permit phone mirroring, and while Rivian’s navigation system is beautifully rendered, the map didn’t seem as up to date as the applications we normally use via Apple CarPlay; for example, it thought a recently reopened highway exit was still closed, which Apple Maps and Waze had updated on the day of.

We found Rivian’s dual-screen setup more intuitive. The Model Y’s single-screen approach requires you to glance to the right to check your speed, which doesn’t feel as natural as a quick peek down at the Rivian’s speedometer. Both cars also show a camera view along the side of the car when you activate the turn signal, and once again the Tesla’s setup makes you look away from the road for longer.

The Rivian’s digital controls are joined by unique multifunction thumbwheels on the steering wheel. They can be pushed in and to either side, as well as scrolled, to control a vast array of functions from volume and drive modes to fan speed and temperature. The breadth of functionality is initially daunting, but using the thumbwheels is pretty intuitive, and we only needed a weekend to memorize the controls.

Moving to the rear, the Rivian’s back seat is palatial. The tall roof and flat floor combine for oodles of space for your head and legs, and the low beltline and glass roof create an open, airy feeling. The Tesla, by comparison, feels a bit cramped for taller adults, with notably less legroom. The sloping roofline cuts into headroom and substantially eats into cargo space. In our testing, we were able to load 10 carry-on suitcases into the Rivian’s rear cargo hold but only seven in the Model Y. The R2 can also roll down its rear glass into the liftgate, just like a Toyota 4Runner.

Tesla makes up for its less spacious back seat by treating rear passengers to their own 8.0-inch touchscreen. The display can not only adjust the heated seats, climate control system, and the audio, but also can be used to play games or stream video. The R2’s rear occupants get a simpler console with air vents and buttons for the heated seats. Both SUVs provide rear passengers with a pair of USB-C ports, with Rivian hiding them in the front seatbacks.

Both SUVs pack dual-motor, all-wheel-drive powertrains. The R2 Performance’s permanent-magnet motors churn out 656 horsepower and 609 pound-feet of torque, and the R2 can decouple the 294-hp front motor via a clutch in the differential. Most of the time the R2 runs in rear-wheel drive, until the rear wheels slip or you demand more performance than the 362-hp rear motor can muster. The Model Y’s powertrain, with an induction motor up front and a permanent-magnet motor at the rear, packs a bit less oomph at 510 horsepower.

Despite the 146-hp gap between the two SUVs, the R2 and Model Y posted remarkably similar numbers at the test track. The Model Y zips to 60 mph in 3.3 seconds with the R2 just two-tenths behind, and the two electric SUVs are neck and neck by the time they reach 80 mph. At the quarter-mile, the Rivian edges in front, completing the run in 11.4 seconds at 126 mph, one-tenth ahead of the Tesla and 4 mph faster. While the R2 tops out at 130 mph, the Model Y keeps going to 153 mph. Both are mega-quick for five-seat SUVs.

The Model Y has a slight advantage in our passing-acceleration test from 30 to 50 mph at 1.6 seconds versus 1.8 seconds for the Rivian, but the R2 is two-tenths quicker from 50 to 70 mph, clocking that jump in 2.1 seconds.

While the acceleration times are extremely similar—and, again, astonishingly swift for five-seat SUVs—the Model Y clearly wins the top-speed race by 20-plus mph.

Things are just as close when it comes to slowing down. Slam on the brakes at 70 mph, and the Tesla comes to a halt in 179 feet; the Rivian needs 178. When stopping from 100 mph, the Model Y holds a six-foot advantage.

HIGHS: Lots of room inside, sophisticated and upscale design, good ride and handling balance.LOWS: Noisy suspension, overly strong regen braking, more power than it can use in the corners.VERDICT: Rivian comes out swinging with a well-designed SUV that drives well and is easy to live with.

The less powerful Model Y’s ability to essentially match the R2’s performance is due in part to its lower curb weight. The Tesla tipped the scales at 4438 pounds, with the Rivian hauling around an extra 547 pounds. This discrepancy also contributes to a big difference on the skidpad. The Rivian, riding on Pirelli Scorpion MS Elect tires, posted 0.81 g, while the Tesla, shod in Hankook Ion Evo AS SUV tires, managed 0.88 g.

We also tested an R2 on the 20-inch wheels and BFGoodrich Trail-Terrain T/A+ tires; it was a tenth quicker to 60 mph and through the quarter-mile. In a surprise twist, the R2 on all-terrain tires also delivered significantly better braking performance, stopping from 70 mph in 166 feet and from 100 mph in 340 feet. Even roadholding improved to 0.84 g.

Numbers don’t tell the full story, however, and the Model Y Performance and R2 Performance feel vastly different from behind the wheel. On a curvy back road, the Tesla is much sportier. It turns in eagerly, the tires provide plenty of grip, and the body stays flat and poised. While the steering isn’t communicative, it is accurate, and the whole package feels taut and agile. The Model Y Performance also feels extremely quick in Insane mode, with a launch befitting the warp-speed badge Tesla sticks on the back. The cornering prowess comes with a trade-off, however. The Tesla pairs adaptive dampers with a coil-spring suspension, and even in the softer Standard setting, the ride is stiff, with every bump transmitted into the cabin. It may be an improvement over the previous Model Y Performance, but the ride is still quite firm.

The Rivian is incredibly zippy in Sport mode, but it doesn’t encourage you to push in the corners the way the Tesla does. The nose points upward when you floor the go-pedal, and there’s more body roll than in the Tesla. The R2 ends up feeling a bit nervous when trying to accelerate forcefully out of a corner. Still, the steering is precise, and the Rivian handles competently, but it instills less confidence in using the full extent of its 656 horsepower in anything other than a straight line.

In normal driving, both the Rivian and the Tesla move briskly and assertively. The Rivian, which also uses coil springs and adaptive dampers, rides noticeably better around town. Although the R2 doesn’t exactly gloss over bumps, impacts are far less intrusive than in the Tesla, as long as you avoid the Firm damper setting. The R2’s suspension can be noisy over rougher pavement, however, and at highway speeds the thunks are accompanied by the rush of wind around the upright A-pillars. At 70 mph, we recorded 67 decibels in the R2’s cabin, one more than in the Model Y. That boxier shape, however, makes for excellent visibility; the Tesla, by contrast, has a tiny slot of a rear window, although the way the Tesla’s nose dips downward provides an expansive view ahead.

HIGHS: Nimble handling, packed with features, Full Self-Driving is getting seriously good.LOWS: It feels like they forgot to finish designing the cabin, ride can be jarring, roofline compromises interior space.VERDICT: The Model Y provides a high-tech, modern experience, but one that’s coldly efficient.

Neither SUV lets you switch regenerative braking fully off. Rivian’s lowest setting is still quite strong, so you’d better like one-pedal driving. Tesla offers two regen braking settings: Standard is quite strong, while Reduced felt like the perfect balance, far less strong than the R2’s weakest setting.

The Rivian is more able to venture off the beaten path. We didn’t take the R2 on anything more challenging than a dirt road, but its 9.6 inches of ground clearance—only one-tenth less than a Jeep Wrangler Sport—and solid approach and departure angles should give owners the confidence to travel farther down the trailhead than the Model Y, with its carlike 6.4 inches of ground clearance.

We also have to talk about, well, not driving. For years, one of Tesla’s unique selling points has been its Full Self-Driving system, and it only gets more impressive each year. While many automakers now offer hands-free driving systems for use on highways, Tesla’s stands out for its ability to take you door to door with zero input required beyond simply plugging in the address; the car takes off, navigating you there swiftly and mostly confidently, even parking at the final destination. Still, we’re not sure FSD really needs a Mad Max setting that allows it to drive up to 85 mph, and we remain unconvinced about using a camera-only system in rain or snow.

Rivian’s Autonomy+ hands-free driving feature isn’t as comprehensive. It doesn’t currently work with the navigation system, but Rivian is planning to add point-to-point capability next year. Currently, it’s best suited to highway driving, where it performs adequately but cautiously. Unlike GM’s latest Super Cruise, Autonomy+ doesn’t automatically change lanes when you come up behind slower traffic, and when you do initiate a lane change via the turn signal stalk, it isn’t the smoothest, getting over quickly with an abrupt steering movement. Even within a lane, it feels a bit more nervous that the Tesla’s system, making many small adjustments in order to stay in between the lines.

The R2 Performance packs an 88-kWh lithium-ion battery, and the EPA estimates 330 miles of range on the 21-inch wheels, with the 20-inch wheels dropping that figure to 307 miles. On our 75-mph highway range test, the R2 maxed out at 260 miles, but the smaller wheels and all-terrain tires slashed range to just 220 miles. The Model Y Performance has 81 kWh of battery capacity, earning a 306-mile range estimate from the EPA. Still, the Tesla managed to beat the Rivian in Car and Driver testing, eking out 270 miles in the 75-mph highway test.

Neither SUV has much of an advantage when it comes to charging. The R2 can hit a peak charging rate of 230 kilowatts, and in our DC fast-charging test, it needed 39 minutes to get from 10 to 90 percent, averaging 119 kilowatts. The Model Y maxes out at 250 kilowatts, and while we weren’t able to test the fast-charging of this Performance trim, a different 2026 Model Y we tested went from 10 to 90 percent in 44 minutes. The R2 is also capable of bidirectional charging, allowing it to power external electronic devices, something this Tesla cannot do.

The battle between the R2 and Model Y is incredibly close. The performance figures are nearly identical, and both SUVs provide adequate range and similar charging speeds. Those who want to carve up back roads will be drawn toward the Model Y’s agility, and Tesla’s Full Self-Driving system remains unmatched. But when it comes to living with the car, the R2’s more compliant ride, more spacious and luxurious cabin, and superior interior ergonomics won us over. While we love crisp driving dynamics as much as anyone, we think the R2 better accomplishes the mission of what a compact SUV should be. The Tesla remains a great option in a crowded segment, but the R2 is coming for the throne.
